newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Santa Claus gets politicised in Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Santa Claus gets politicised in Sarajevo.

text.p: Santa Claus has stumbled into Bosnia's political fray this holiday season.
No longer merely a jovial symbol of good cheer, Santa Claus has found himself the subject of solemn political and religious discussion in the Bosnian capital.
Sarajevo traditionally celebrates New Year's eve with the Bosnian version of Santa Claus, "Grandfather Frost", who delivers gifts to children of all faiths.
But after a vicious war that played on religious differences between Moslems, Roman Catholic Croats and Orthodox Christian Serbs, Grandfather Frost's traditional role is being questioned.
The issue became less than a laughing matter when two journalists were beaten up last week after their independent radio station asked listeners if Grandfather Frost was being unduly "politicised".
The journalists alleged the beating was carried out by activists for the main Moslem nationalist party, the Party of Democratic Action (SDA).
The SDA was forced to issue a statement saying it had never tried to bar Grandfather Frost from public celebrations.

Whatever the motives behind the attack, many Sarajevans have been eager to promote Grandfather Frost since Moslem President Alija Izetbegovic complained last January that Santa Claus was an alien symbol that had no place on state television.
Izetbegovic, a devout Moslem, criticised New Year's celebrations last year as "heartless" at a time when many Bosnians were still grieving from the war.
His letter said the fact that Bosnia was a European country did not mean it had to open its doors "to all European vices, alcohol, pornography, drugs and to libertines of all sorts".
Aides to Izetbegovic have taken pains this month to reassure reporters that authorities have nothing against Grandfather Frost -- officially or unofficially.
The highest Islamic religious leader in Bosnia, Reis-ul-ulema, weighed in on Santa's significance with a statement published on Christmas Eve.

He upheld the right of Bosnians to exercise their religious freedom but he made clear that Grandfather Frost was not accepted as a symbol for Moslems. "Using other symbols as your own is not a symbol of high culture. To love your symbols and respect others' is the moral duty of every sensible man," Reis-ul-ulema wrote.
For Sarajevans who take their religion less seriously, talk about Grandfather Frost's appropriate role seems out of place for a city that boasts of its centuries-old cultural mix.
One Sarajevan felt so strongly about Grandfather Frost that he dressed up a young boy as Santa and paraded him around town to hand out sweets this week.
Hamza Baksic, a former editor at the daily Oslobodjenje, said he was confident Grandfather Frost was alive and well despite the debate raging around him.
"The Santa Claus character is a custom that dates back for centuries," Baksic told Reuters.

"That tradition is completely harmless and represents only joy for children...This is only a momentary caprice and such a long tradition cannot be stopped like that. I am sure this is only temporary."
